b: I work in a very laid-back office. We have hybrid/remote, and everyone uses the remote option whenever possible. There really is no reason for anyone to be in the office, but the company insists. I don’t know why.

My section of the office has just one bathroom, which is not terribly convenient. Recently, I was using said bathroom when someone tried to open the door (it was locked). When I was done, I left the bathroom to see one of my coworkers puking into the trash.
This coworker warned me some time ago that they have a nervous condition that sometimes leads to barfing. They said that they carry a bag with them in case a crisis hits.

I want to be sympathetic — they can’t help it — but why are they working in-office with something like this? I don’t know if they asked HR for remote privileges and were denied, or if they were too embarrassed to ask. I used to have severe emetophobia (fear of vomiting), and though it has improved, this is not something I want to see (and I’m sure nobody else in the office wants to see it either).
Here are some of my concerns:
They might not make it to the bathroom, even when it’s empty. This would create a huge mess for the cleaning staff to clean up. In the meantime, it would just sit there.

They might have a virus that was causing them to get sick, but would think that it was the nervous condition causing it. This means that they could come to work sick and expose the office to said virus. (As it happens, they have come to work with the after-effects of a heavy cold more than once.)
They might lose it when someone in the office is on a call, providing unwelcome sound effects in the background.
They might lose it when a VIP is visiting the office.

How do I approach HR about this? It’s entirely possible that they don’t know about the problem. I’m also torn because this coworker is a very nice person, and would undoubtedly know that I went to HR if HR contacts them about this issue.
This is your coworker’s medical condition to handle.

If one of the items on your list happens, they will handle it at that point. None of what you listed is so dire that steps must be taken to prevent it at all costs … and it’s probably pretty unlikely. It sounds like your coworker heads for the bathroom when they feel nausea coming on, which is appropriate. If the bathroom is occupied, they have a back-up plan — which isn’t ideal, but isn’t enough of a disaster that you need to go to HR with their personal medical info.

Keep in mind that what you listed could happen to anyone. Someone could get food poisoning or sudden illness and not make it to the bathroom. Someone might be pregnant and vomiting on the reg! In fact, pregnant people with morning sickness are pretty common, and most offices never have to deal with someone vomiting in the background of a call or barfing on a VP!
I think you’ve got to consider that your emetophobia may be coloring your thinking here.
In any case, this is not something where you need to alert HR. (It’s also probably not a condition where the company would be required to offer full-time work-from-home as an accommodation anyway.)
